Attachment I 
Panel Testimony and exhibit of Brian McNierney, 
Carol Teixeira, Yan Flishenbaum, and Stacy Powers

I. 
INTRODUCTION 
Q. 
MR. MCNIERNEY, PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.   
A. 
My name is Brian McNierney.  My business address is 18 Link Drive, Binghamton, New 
York 13902.  
Q. 
MR. MCNIERNEY, BY WHOM ARE YOU EMPLOYED AND IN WHAT 
CAPACITY? 
A.  
I am employed by Rochester Gas & Electric Corporation (“RG&E”) as Director – 
Regulatory for both RG&E and New York State Electric & Gas Corporation (“NYSEG”).   
Q. 
MR. MCNIERNEY, WHAT ARE YOUR AREAS OF RESPONSIBILITY IN THIS 
POSITION? 
A. 
I am responsible for electric rate calculations, and rate design for NYSEG and RG&E as 
well as representing NYSEG and RG&E in various rate and regulatory proceedings. 
Q. 
MR. MCNIERNEY, PLEASE BRIEFLY DESCRIBE YOUR EDUCATIONAL 
BACKGROUND AND EMPLOYMENT EXPERIENCE.  
A. 
In 1986, I graduated from St. Bonaventure University with a Bachelor of Business 
Administration.  I began my employment at NYSEG and RG&E in 2000 as a Lead Analyst 
in Electric Supplier Services.  Over the years since then, I have held several positions 
within the Companies and have been in the Regulatory Department since 2013. 
Q. 
MR. MCNIERNEY, HAVE YOU PREVIOUSLY TESTIFIED IN REGULATORY 
PROCEEDINGS?  
A. 
Yes, I have submitted testimony in New York Public Service Commission (“NYPSC” or 
“PSC”) Cases 15-E-5 0283 et al., Cases 19-E-0378 6 et al., Cases 22-E-0317 7 et al. and 
Cases 25-E-0375 et al.

Attachment I 
Page 3 of 29 
 
 
Q.  
MS. TEIXEIRA, PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.  
A.  
My name is Carol Teixeira.  My business address is 300 Erie Boulevard West, Syracuse, 
New York 13202. 
Q.  
MS. TEIXEIRA, BY WHOM ARE YOU EMPLOYED AND IN WHAT CAPACITY?  
A.  
I am employed by the National Grid USA Service Company, Inc. (“National Grid Service 
Company”), a subsidiary of National Grid USA (“National Grid”), as Manager of New 
York Electric Pricing.  I am responsible for supervising the study, analysis, and design of 
delivery service rates, rate contracts, surcharge adjustment factors, riders, and terms and 
condition of service for National Grid’s utility, Niagara Mohawk Power Corporation d/b/a 
National Grid (“NMPC” or “Niagara Mohawk”), including developing tariffs and 
testimony supporting such rates before the NYPSC. 
Q.  
MS. TEIXEIRA, PLEASE DESCRIBE YOUR EDUCATIONAL BACKGROUND.  
A.  
In 1989, I graduated from Syracuse University with a Bachelor of Science in Electrical 
Engineering.  In 2007, I received my Master of Business Administration from LeMoyne 
College. 
Q.  
MS. TEIXEIRA, PLEASE DESCRIBE YOUR PROFESSIONAL BACKGROUND.  
A.  
I first joined Niagara Mohawk in 1989 when I was hired as an Assistant/Junior Engineer, 
Instrumentation Control and Design, where I was responsible for the design and installation 
of control and instrumentation systems at Niagara Mohawk’s fossil generating stations.  
From 1997 to 2002, I served as a Power Contract Specialist at Niagara Mohawk in various 
departments, including Unregulated Generation, Transmission Scheduling, and Customer 
Contract Services, where I was responsible for different aspects of power purchase 
agreements and other supply contracts with generators and customers interconnected to

Attachment I 
Page 4 of 29 
 
 
Niagara Mohawk’s system.  From 2002 to 2005, I was a Senior/Principal Analyst, Electric 
Pricing at Niagara Mohawk, with responsibility for developing and administrating Niagara 
Mohawk’s flexible retail electric contracts for large commercial and industrial customers.  
I became Transmission Account Manager, Transmission Commercial Services in 2005, 
where I had responsibility for managing the Company’s interconnection process in 
compliance with Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”) 
policies and orders and acting as primary contact for wholesale generators interconnecting 
to National Grid’s transmission system in both New York and New England.  In 2008, I 
was promoted to Manager, Load Research and Analysis.  My responsibilities in this 
position included preparation of load research studies to support electric rate cases, 
customer retail billing, settlement, and special studies for all National Grid companies and 
the Long Island Power Authority (“LIPA”), as well as overseeing survey meter design 
sample studies for all companies and ensuring a sufficient sample of survey meters in the 
field to support load studies.  I became the Manager of Billing Project Management 
Services in 2011, with responsibility for support and operations of customer billing for all 
National Grid companies and LIPA.  I took my current position as Manager, New York 
Electric Pricing in May 2014.   
Q.  
MS. 
TEIXEIRA, 
HAVE YOU 
PREVIOUSLY 
TESTIFIED 
BEFORE A 
REGULATORY COMMISSION? 
A.  
Yes.  I testified before the NYPSC in support of the electric rate proposals in the NMPC’s 
2017 electric rate case (Case 17-E-0238), the NMPC 2020 rate case (Case 20-E-0380) and 
the NMPC 2024 rate case (Case 24-E-0322).  In addition, I have testified on behalf of

Attachment I 
Page 5 of 29 
 
 
National Grid in support of the NMPC Wholesale Distribution Services tariff, filed with 
FERC on October 2, 2026, in Docket No. ER27-31, which is pending approval. 
Q.  
MR. FLISHENBAUM, PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.  
A.  
My name is Yan Flishenbaum.  My business address is 4 Irving Place, New York, NY 
10003. 
Q.  
MR. FLISHENBAUM, BY WHOM ARE YOU EMPLOYED AND IN WHAT 
CAPACITY? 
A.  
I am employed by Consolidated Edison Company of New York, Inc. (“Con Edison”).   
Q.  
MR. FLISHENBAUM, WHAT ARE YOUR AREAS OF RESPONSIBILITY IN THIS 
POSITION?  
A.  
I currently serve as Director of Con Edison’s Rate Engineering Department. 
Q.  
MR. FLISHENBAUM, PLEASE BRIEFLY DESCRIBE YOUR EDUCATIONAL 
BACKGROUND AND EMPLOYMENT EXPERIENCE.  
A.  
I received a Bachelor of Business Administration in Economics from Pace University in 
2001 and a Master of Business Administration in Finance and Economics from New York 
University in 2008.  I began my career in 2001 in the Cost Analysis area of the Rate 
Engineering Department.  In 2003, I was promoted to Analyst, where I focused on 
developing costing methodologies related to unbundling.  I advanced to Senior Analyst in 
2005, and in 2008, became a Senior Rate Analyst and was responsible for developing the 
Company’s cost-of-service models.  In 2013, I was promoted to Section Manager of the 
Electric Rates area of the Rate Engineering Department.  I later served as a Department 
Manager for the Load Research and Cost of Service group, as well as a Department

Attachment I 
Page 6 of 29 
 
 
Manager of the Orange and Rockland Rates section.  I assumed my current role as Director 
of the Rate Engineering Department in 2025. 
Q.  
MR. FLISHENBAUM, HAVE YOU PREVIOUSLY TESTIFIED IN REGULATORY 
PROCEEDINGS?  
A.  
Yes.  I have filed testimony before the NYPSC and the New Jersey Board of Public 
Utilities. 
Q.  
MS. POWERS, PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.  
A.  
My name is Stacy Powers.  My business address is 284 South Avenue, Poughkeepsie, New 
York 12601. 
Q.  
MS. POWERS, BY WHOM ARE YOU EMPLOYED AND IN WHAT CAPACITY?  
A.  
I am employed by Central Hudson Gas & Electric Corporation (“Central Hudson”) as 
Director – Regulatory Forecasts & Planning.    
Q.  
MS. POWERS, WHAT ARE YOUR AREAS OF RESPONSIBILITY IN THIS 
POSITION?  
A.  
I am responsible for cost studies, rates, tariffs, revenue requirements and regulatory 
compliance.  
Q.  
MS. POWERS, PLEASE BRIEFLY DESCRIBE YOUR EDUCATIONAL 
BACKGROUND AND EMPLOYMENT EXPERIENCE.  
A.  
I received a Bachelor of Science degree in Business Administration and Accounting from 
Marist College in 2006 and a Master of Business Administration from Marist College in 
2010.  I have served in various capacities of increasing responsibility in the rates and 
regulatory area of Central Hudson since 2006.

Attachment I 
Page 7 of 29 
 
 
Q.  
MS. POWERS, HAVE YOU PREVIOUSLY TESTIFIED IN REGULATORY 
PROCEEDINGS?  
A.  
Yes, I have filed testimony before the NYPSC.  
Q. 
ON WHOSE BEHALF ARE YOU ALL TESTIFYING?  
A. 
We are testifying on behalf of Central Hudson, Con Edison, NYSEG, NMPC, Orange and 
Rockland Utilities, Inc. (“O&R”), and RG&E (collectively, “Indicated New York 
Transmission Owners” or “Indicated NYTOs” and individually, “Transmission Owner”) as 
rates subject matter expert representatives.   
Q. 
WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF THIS TESTIMONY?  
A. 
The purpose of our testimony is to support the Indicated NYTOs’ proposed revisions to 
Section 5 of the New York Independent System Operator, Inc. (“NYISO”) Open Access 
Transmission Tariff (“ISO OATT”), which the Indicated NYTOs are submitting pursuant 
to section 205 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”) in response to the Commission’s June 18, 
2026 order in Docket No. EL26-69-000.1  Revised Section 5 continues the practice that has 
been in effect since the NYISO commenced operation in 1999.  Under revised Section 5, 
Large Loads or Eligible Customers serving Large Loads, including Eligible Customers 
taking the new Firm and Non-Firm Withdrawal Service that the NYISO is proposing in its 
companion section 205 filing, will pay the existing retail delivery rates approved by the 
NYPSC or, in the case of LIPA, by the LIPA Board of Trustees.  The Indicated NYTOs are 
not proposing new rates.  Instead, revised Section 5 references the applicable delivery 
service classifications for each Transmission Owner, as approved by the NYPSC or the 
LIPA Board of Trustees, as applicable.  Our testimony explains the history of Section 5, 
 
1  
N.Y. Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 195 FERC ¶ 61,216 (2026) (“Show Cause Order”).

Attachment I 
Page 8 of 29 
 
 
how bundled New York delivery rates are developed and collected, how those rates are 
voltage-differentiated and offer Large Loads meaningful choices, and why a separate 
transmission-only rate for Large Loads at this time would be potentially harmful.  
Q. 
ARE YOU ALL SPONSORING ANY EXHIBITS IN CONNECTION WITH THIS 
TESTIMONY?  
A. 
Yes.  On behalf of the Indicated NYTOs,2 we are sponsoring the following exhibits, which 
are attached to and made a part of our testimony:  Exhibit A – The NYTOs’ PSC Delivery 
Rates of the Applicable Transmission Owner to Large Loads.  
II. 
HISTORICAL BACKGROUND 
Q. 
WHEN DID RETAIL ACCESS BEGIN IN NEW YORK RELATIVE TO THE 
START OF THE NYISO’S OPERATIONS? 
A. 
The PSC adopted retail access programs in 1996.  Under retail access, electric commodity 
supply was unbundled from transmission and distribution service for eligible retail 
customers and the energy service companies (“ESCOs”) serving them.  Retail access 
programs permit eligible retail customers to choose a competitive supplier or ESCO for the 
commodity while the local utility continues to provide the delivery function over its 
transmission and distribution system.  Delivery rates applicable to this form of “retail 
wheeling” or “retail transmission service” are deliveries of third-party supplied energy to 
retail customers in New York.3   
 
2  
As a non-jurisdictional utility, LIPA is not a respondent to the Show Cause Order and its rates and charges 
for transmission service are reviewed and approved by LIPA’s Board of Trustees under applicable state law.  Where 
addressed in this testimony, the discussion of LIPA’s delivery service classifications and related rates and charges is 
solely for informational purposes. 
3  
Case 94-E-0952, et al., Opinion No. 96-12 (issued and eff. May 20, 1996).

Attachment I 
Page 9 of 29 
 
 
As part of the development of the initial ISO OATT, Section 5 of the ISO OATT was 
developed to address already State-approved retail access programs, and it identified the 
rates and charges under which retail access customers would receive service.  FERC 
accepted Section 5 as part of the tariff filing effective at the start of the NYISO’s operations 
in 1999.4   
Q. 
HOW HAS SECTION 5 FUNCTIONED SINCE THE NYISO BEGAN 
OPERATIONS? 
A. 
Since the NYISO was formed, Section 5 of the ISO OATT has referenced each 
Transmission Owner’s PSC-approved retail access tariff or, for LIPA, the rates and terms 
established under State law, as the respective retail tariffs may be amended from time-to-
time.  Section 5 provides that the rates, terms, and conditions for retail access service are 
those set in the applicable retail tariff, and that the Transmission Owner bills and collects 
those charges in accordance with that tariff.  The Commission accepted these provisions in 
1999.5  In this way, the PSC has set the retail delivery rates for each of the Indicated 
NYTOs, and the ISO OATT has incorporated such rates by reference.  This cooperative 
federalism arrangement has worked for the entire life of the NYISO, approximately 27 
years. 
 
 
4  
Cent. Hudson Gas & Elec. Corp., 86 FERC ¶ 61,062, order on reh’g and compliance, 88 FERC ¶ 61,138 
(1999). 
5  
Id.

Attachment I 
Page 10 of 29 
 
 
III. 
NYPSC BUNDLED DELIVERY RATES 
Q. 
HOW DO THE INDICATED NYTOS RECOVER THEIR TRANSMISSION AND 
DISTRIBUTION COSTS FROM RETAIL CUSTOMERS? 
A. 
Central Hudson, Con Edison, NYSEG, NMPC, O&R, and RG&E recover their 
transmission and distribution costs through bundled delivery rates set by the PSC.  Through 
many proceedings, the PSC has unbundled the power supply function from delivery 
service.  Capacity and energy supply are therefore not priced and billed under the 
Transmission Owner’s retail tariff delivery rates, and the retail customers either take 
unbundled supply from the Transmission Owner pursuant to its Provider of Last Resort 
(“POLR”) obligation or enter into separate purchases from a competitive load-serving 
entity (“LSE”), which several PSC-approved tariffs call an ESCO.  Retail customers may 
also function as their own ESCO.  While the commodity supply (capacity and energy) is 
unbundled from the delivery rates, the delivery rates remain bundled for the most part, even 
though they are voltage-differentiated based on cost allocations which intentionally remove 
certain distribution costs from the rates developed for transmission-level customers.  There 
is, however, no separate retail rate consisting only of transmission-related costs.  The 
Delivery rates are recovered, together with distribution, metering, customer service, and 
overhead costs, through the customer and demand charges of each service classification. 
Q. 
WHY DOES THE BUNDLED NATURE OF THE NYPSC’S DELIVERY RATES 
MATTER HERE? 
A. 
There is no stand-alone, transmission-only retail rate in New York that could be applied to 
Large Loads.  The transmission component of retail delivery service is embedded in rates 
that the PSC approved to recover each utility’s total delivery revenue requirement from all

Attachment I 
Page 11 of 29 
 
 
retail customer classes.  A Large Load connecting at transmission voltage will take service 
under one of these classifications.  A Large Load customer’s charges will therefore reflect 
transmission costs together with its fair share of other delivery costs, as the PSC has 
determined.   
IV. 
THE NYPSC RATEMAKING PROCESS 
Q. 
PLEASE DESCRIBE THE NYPSC RATE CASE PROCESS. 
A. 
A rate case typically begins when the utility files proposed tariff changes with the NYPSC, 
together with testimony and exhibits supporting its revenue requirement.  The revenue 
requirement covers all the costs of running the delivery business, including operation and 
maintenance expense, administrative and general expense, depreciation, taxes, and a return 
on rate base, and it is recovered through base delivery rates.  Certain items, such as the 
System Benefits Charge (“SBC”), are separated out and billed through surcharges rather 
than base rates. 
 
The utility also files an embedded cost of service (“ECOS”) study and rate design 
testimony.  The ECOS study is used as a guide as part of the rate design process to allocate 
the revenue requirement among service classes.  The rate design testimony proposes how 
each service class’s share will be recovered through customer charges, demand charges, 
energy charges, and time-of-use or other rate features.  
Q. 
WHO PARTICIPATES IN AN NYPSC RATE CASE? 
A. 
The Staff of the Department of Public Service (“DPS Staff”) participates as a party in every 
major rate case.  Other parties may also intervene, typically including the Utility 
Intervention Unit of the New York State Department of State, city agencies, municipalities, 
elected officials, large industrial and commercial customer associations, advocates for low-

Attachment I 
Page 12 of 29 
 
 
income customers, ESCOs and their trade associations, environmental advocates, and 
others.  These parties represent a wide range of customer classes and interests, including 
the interests of high-voltage, high load-factor customers. 
Q.  
HOW DO PARTIES TYPICALLY PARTICIPATE IN A NYPSC RATE CASE? 
A. 
The parties conduct extensive discovery through information requests, and DPS Staff (and 
at times other intervenors) file responsive testimony.  The utility may file rebuttal 
testimony.  Contested issues may be tried in evidentiary hearings before PSC 
Administrative Law Judges (“ALJs”), at which parties may introduce direct testimony and 
exhibits and witnesses may be cross-examined.  The ALJs may issue a recommended 
decision, and parties may file briefs and exceptions before the PSC acts. 
Q. 
DO MOST RATE CASES PROCEED TO A FULLY LITIGATED DECISION? 
A. 
No.  Most rate cases are resolved through multi-party settlement negotiations that produce 
a joint proposal.  Settlement negotiations are conducted under the PSC’s settlement 
procedures, and all parties have an opportunity to participate.  A joint proposal typically 
resolves the revenue requirement, cost allocation, and rate design for every service class at 
once.  It reflects negotiated exchanges of consideration, in which parties accept outcomes 
on some issues in return for outcomes on others.   
Q. 
HOW DOES THE PSC REVIEW A JOINT PROPOSAL? 
A. 
The PSC does not simply accept a joint proposal because the parties have agreed to it.  It 
reviews the joint proposal under its settlement guidelines, which consider, among other 
things, whether the settlement is consistent with law and PSC policy; whether it produces 
results within the range of reasonable outcomes that would likely arise from litigation; 
whether it balances the interests of ratepayers, investors, and the long-term viability of the

Attachment I 
Page 13 of 29 
 
 
utility; and whether it is supported by testimony and evidence submitted in the formal 
record.6  The PSC may review items such as testimony, evidence, statements in support 
from the parties, and, if applicable a recommended decision, submitted in the formal record 
to support its rate order.   
Q. 
HOW DOES THE PSC RATEMAKING PROCESS CONCLUDE? 
A. 
The PSC issues a final order adopting, modifying, or rejecting the joint proposal, or 
resolving litigated issues, and directs the utility to file compliance tariffs.  
Q. 
DID THE CURRENT RATES OF THE INDICATED NYTOS RESULT FROM 
SETTLEMENTS? 
A. 
Yes.  The current rates of Central Hudson, Con Edison, NMPC, and O&R are based on 
PSC-approved settlements rather than fully litigated orders.  These rate plans generally run 
for three years.  The rate plans may be extended pending new rate filings, or continued 
under temporary rates set by the PSC.  NYSEG and RG&E are currently operating under 
a temporary rate order issued in May 2026 as they continue settlement negotiations in their 
ongoing rate case.  
V. 
CURRENT RATES AND CHARGES  
Q. 
HAVE THE RATE DESIGNS FOR TRANSMISSION-VOLTAGE CUSTOMERS 
BEEN DEVELOPED OVER TIME? 
A. 
Yes.  The service classifications available to transmission-voltage customers, including 
standby and optional demand rates, have been refined or resulted from an evolutionary 
process over many individual utility rate cases and statewide proceedings and many years.  
 
6  
Procedural Guidelines for Settlements, Cases 90-M-0255 et al. (1992).

Attachment I 
Page 14 of 29 
 
 
Each iteration was refined through discovery, testimony, and negotiation among parties 
representing all customer classes, and each was approved by the PSC. 
Q. 
WHAT CHARGES DO TRANSMISSION-VOLTAGE DELIVERY CUSTOMERS 
PAY PURSUANT TO PSC-APPROVED TARIFFS? 
A. 
Base delivery rates for these classes generally consist of a monthly customer charge plus a 
per-kW demand charge.  In addition, delivery customers pay a series of PSC-authorized 
pass-through surcharges, including the SBC and taxes.  Depending on who serves as the 
customer’s LSE, the customer or its LSE also pays supply-related charges.  
Q. 
MR. MCNIERNEY, DOES A TRANSMISSION-VOLTAGE SERVICE CLASS PAY 
ONLY FOR TRANSMISSION COSTS? 
A. 
No.  Customers in a transmission-voltage service class pay more than transmission charges 
alone.  For example, under NYSEG’s latest ECOS study for retail delivery service, 
approximately two-thirds of the transmission service class’s allocated costs are 
transmission-related.  The remaining one-third is an allocable share of other delivery, 
metering, call center, and similar overhead costs that the utility incurs to serve all 
customers. 
Q. 
PLEASE DESCRIBE THE PSC-AUTHORIZED DELIVERY SURCHARGES. 
A. 
Each Indicated Transmission Owner has several PSC-authorized surcharges that apply to 
its delivery load regardless of who serves as the customer’s LSE.  All Indicated NYTOs 
have identical or similar surcharges, with some variation, and some surcharges are unique 
to particular companies.  Electric surcharges are adjustments added to or subtracted from 
a customer’s bill to account for certain costs that are not included in the base electric rates.

Attachment I 
Page 15 of 29 
 
 
Q. 
HOW ARE THE SBC AND THE COSTS OF ZERO-EMISSION CREDITS 
COLLECTED? 
A. 
The components of the SBC related to cost recovery for the program budgets of the New 
York State Energy Research and Development Authority (“NYSERDA”) are split among 
the utilities on a load ratio share basis and billed to delivery customers as a per-kWh charge.  
On the other hand, zero-emission credit (“ZEC”) costs are handled differently.  NYSERDA 
informs each LSE of its ZEC-related obligation.  Each utility then sets an annual per-kWh 
rate that it bills to each utility’s respective commodity customers.  Presumably, other non-
utility LSEs then  charge their allocated ZEC costs to their retail customers.  
Q. 
WHAT IS THE ROLE OF THE WHOLESALE TRANSMISSION SERVICE 
CHARGE UNDER ATTACHMENT H OF THE NYISO OATT? 
A. 
Pursuant to Section 14.1 of Attachment H, the wholesale Transmission Service Charge 
(“TSC”) is of limited application and applies primarily to “wheel through” and “export” 
transactions that exit the New York Control Area.  The wholesale TSC does not apply to 
retail delivery and Transmission Services within the NYISO, including the NYISO’s new 
proposed Firm and Non-Firm Withdrawal Services applicable to retail customers, which 
are PSC-established rates in Section 5 of the ISO OATT. 
VI. 
VOLTAGE DIFFERENTIATION OF PSC-APPROVED DELIVERY RATES 
Q.

THE

Q. 
HAVE EACH OF THE INDICATED TOS PROVIDED THE SERVICE  
CLASSIFICATIONS IN EXHIBIT A? 
A. 
Yes.   
Q. 
MR. MCNIERNEY, ARE THE PSC-APPROVED DELIVERY RATES THAT WILL 
APPLY TO LARGE LOADS DIFFERENTIATED BY VOLTAGE? 
A. 
Yes.  For example, for NYSEG’s PSC service classification SC 7, Large General Service 
with Time-of-Use Metering, there are three currently available voltages (SC 7-1, 7-2, and 
7-4):  7-1 – Secondary, 120–480 volts; 7-2 – Primary, 2.4–34.5 kV or regulated 46 kV; and 
7-4 – Transmission, 115 kV and above.  
Q.  
MR. MCNIERNEY, WHAT ARE THE RATES FOR HIGHER VOLTAGE 
CUSTOMERS? 
A. 
Yes.  For example, for NYSEG’s PSC service classification SC 7, Large General Service 
with Time-of-Use Metering, the applicable demand charge (per kW) for each one of those 
voltages classifications is currently: 7-1 – $14.55; 7-2 – $13.76; and 7-4 – $2.07. 
 Q. 
MR. MCNIERNEY, CAN YOU PROVIDE A HYPOTHETICAL EXAMPLE OF 
WHAT THE RESULTING CHARGE WOULD BE FOR A LARGE LOAD UNDER 
NYSEG’S PSC SERVICE CLASSIFICATION SC 7, ASSUMING A 100 MW LOAD 
AND 73,000 MWH PER MONTH UNDER THE LOWEST AND HIGHEST 
VOLTAGE RATES? 
A. 
Yes.  A 100 MW Large Load with 73,000 MWh of energy consumption for a given month 
would have demand charges under NYSEG’s PSC service classification SC 7: 7-1 of 
$1,455,000 compared to $207,000 under NYSEG’s transmission voltage level demand 
charge 7-4 rate.  I do not mean to imply that it is plausible to assume a 100 MW load would

Attachment I 
Page 18 of 29 
 
 
connect at distribution voltage.  But the application of the distribution demand charge 
versus the highest voltage level rate illustrates how substantially lower the rate and charges 
would be under the transmission level rate compared to the distribution rate.   
Q. 
MS. TEIXEIRA, DOES NIAGARA MOHAWK HAVE SIMILAR VOLTAGE 
DIFFERENTIATION? 
A.  
Yes.  NMPC electric rates have voltage differentiated delivery rates for all of its large 
commercial and industrial service classes.  The voltage delivery levels for which distinct 
delivery rates apply are for customers connected to the NMPC distribution system at 
Secondary (0 – 2.2 kV), Primary (2.2 kV – 15 kV), Sub-transmission (22 kV – 50 kV) and 
Transmission (Over 60 kV).  The Large Load customers at issue in this proceeding would 
be billed at SC3A or parent SC3A delivery rates at the Transmission voltage delivery 
level.    
Q.  
MS. TEIXEIRA, CONTINUING WITH NMPC, ARE THE RATES FOR HIGHER 
VOLTAGE CUSTOMERS CONSIDERABLY LOWER THAN THE LOWER 
VOLTAGE DISTRIBUTION RATES?  
A. 
For a customer billed at standard SC3A rates, the customer would pay a much lower 
demand charge of $4.89 per maximum kW in the billing period at the Transmission level 
than:  the $15.58 per maximum kW at the Secondary or Primary level and $5.42 at the Sub-
transmission level.  The monthly customer charge is higher at the Transmission level than 
at lower voltage levels but for a large load customer the customer charge would be an 
insignificant portion of their monthly bill compared to the demand charge (approximately 
2% for a 100 MW large load customer, for example).  See below for an example:

Attachment I 
Page 19 of 29 
 
 
 
Q.  
MS. TEIXEIRA, 
DO 
SC3A TRANSMISSION 
RATES 
INCLUDE ANY 
DISTRIBUTION-RELATED CHARGES? 
A.  
Yes, but only to a limited extent.  SC3A Transmission rates are primarily composed of 
transmission-related costs.  However, Niagara Mohawk’s Embedded Cost of Service Study 
also allocates a small amount of distribution-related costs to SC3A Transmission 
customers, including costs associated with metering, customer programs, and 
administrative functions.  These costs are minimal relative to the overall cost allocation, 
with the vast majority of costs allocated to SC3A Transmission customers being 
transmission-related. 
Q.  
MS. TEIXEIRA, CAN YOU PROVIDE A HYPOTHETICAL EXAMPLE OF WHAT

Q. 
DO LARGE LOADS HAVE FLEXIBILITY TO CHOOSE AMONG SERVICE 
CLASSIFICATIONS? 
A. 
Yes, generally speaking.  In accordance with applicable procedures for delivery service, 
Large Loads and their LSEs may choose among the applicable classifications identified in 
revised OATT Section 5.2.8.  For all of the Indicated NYTOs, these include a standard 
transmission-voltage or large general service classification, a standby service classification 
and, for all Indicated NYTOs, an optional demand service classification.  The customer can 
generally select the classification that makes the most sense given its load profile, although 
there may be instances in which the applicability criteria of the tariff limit some of the 
options available. 
Q. 
HOW DO THESE CLASSIFICATIONS ACCOMMODATE A LARGE LOAD 
THAT IS CURTAILED OR REDUCES ITS WITHDRAWALS VOLUNTARILY? 
A. 
Under the PSC-approved rate classifications, standby and optional demand rates include 
daily as-used demand charges.  Under these designs, the customer’s demand charges reflect 
its actual demand during each daily peak or super-peak period rather than a single monthly 
maximum.  A high load-factor Large Load that is curtailed by the NYISO, or that 
voluntarily reduces its withdrawals during the peak hours on any day, will pay lower 
demand charges for that day.

Attachment I 
Page 21 of 29 
 
 
Q. 
WOULD THE LARGE LOAD RECEIVE THE SAME RATE REDUCTION 
BENEFIT REGARDLESS OF WHETHER IT IS CURTAILED BY THE NYISO OR 
A UTILITY, OR IT VOLUNTARILY REDUCES ITS WITHDRAWALS? 
A. 
Yes.  Any Large Load demand reduction would produce the same rate reduction benefit 
whether it is directed by the NYISO or a utility, or it is the result of a voluntary reduction. 
Q. 
MR. MCNIERNEY, ARE THERE RATE OPTIONS THAT COULD ALLOW A 
FLEXIBLE LARGE LOAD TO LOWER ITS MONTHLY DELIVERY BILL BY 
REDUCING ITS DAILY PEAK DEMAND? 
A. 
Yes.  NYSEG, as well as other Indicated NYTOs, offer Optional Demand Service/Standby 
Service which can apply to a Large Load customer.  For example, with Optional Demand 
Service/Standby Service, the conventional monthly non-coincident demand-charge 
structure is replaced with a monthly contract demand charge and daily “as-used demand” 
charges.  The Optional Demand Service/Standby as-used charges depend on the Large 
Load customer’s measured demand during defined “On-Peak” and “Super-Peak” periods 
whereas the standard Transmission level service class, by contrast, is based on monthly 
non-coincident peak demand.  Accordingly, under Optional Demand Service/Standby, a 
significant portion of demand-related charges depend on what the Large Load customer 
does during these applicable periods (On-Peak and Super-Peak) on each day. 
Q. 
MR. MCNIERNEY, CAN YOU PROVIDE A HYPOTHETICAL EXAMPLE OF 
HOW A FLEXIBLE LARGE LOAD CAN LOWER ITS MONTHLY DELIVERY 
BILL UNDER NYSEG’S SC 15, OPTIONAL DEMAND SERVICE? 
A. 
Yes.  Consider an example in which a Large Load is curtailed by the NYISO or a utility to 
zero for five weekdays during the billing period.  Since as-used demand charges are based

Attachment I

on the sum of the daily On-Peak or Super-Peak demand during the billing period, a 
curtailment for a day reduces the On-Peak or Super-Peak demand by one day.  In a month 
that has 20 days in which On-Peak demand is measured, at current NYSEG rates, a 
customer with 100 MW load in all peak hours would have an On-Peak as-used demand of 
20 X 100 MW = 2,000 MW.  If five days had no as-used demand due to curtailment, the 
On-Peak as-used demand for the month would be 1,500 MW.  For a Large Load customer 
that would otherwise take service under the NYSEG SC 7-4 rate, at the current NYSEG 
SC 15 On-Peak daily as-used rate of $0.06030 per kW, there would be a reduction of 
$30,150 in charges.  The reduction would be greater in months that had Super-Peak daily 
as-used demand in addition to On-Peak daily as-used demand.

Q. 
WHAT PROBLEMS COULD OCCUR IF THE INDICATED NYTOS’ EXISTING 
DELIVERY 
RATES 
AND 
PSC 
RATEMAKING 
PROCESSES 
WERE 
DISTURBED? 
A. 
In the case of settled rates, isolating the transmission component in the Indicated NYTOs’ 
PSC-approved delivery service could potentially undermine the associated settlements and 
the exchanges of consideration that the settlement parties made to reach them.  In the case 
of litigated rates, FERC action could upset rates determined following the conclusion of 
extensive procedures.  Each joint proposal resolves the revenue requirement, cost 
allocation, and rate design for all classes as a package.  Isolating the transmission 
component of one class’s rate could potentially leave the remaining costs, including that 
class’s share of distribution, metering, customer service, and overhead costs, to be 
reallocated.  Changing rates for one or a few classes in isolation could potentially shift 
costs among classes and violate revenue neutrality, potentially producing unjust and 
unreasonable rates for other customers, including for residential and small commercial

Attachment I 
Page 24 of 29 
 
 
customers.  Moreover, the Indicated NYTOs could have to re-open retail settlements to 
adjust existing rate classes in a revenue-neutral manner.  That process would require a 
significant, administratively inefficient undertaking, and would create needless uncertainty 
for all rate classes.  Further, to the extent that certain subsections of customers are not 
included in the forecasts used to develop rates, there may need to be extensive rate changes.   
Q. 
HOW WOULD A SEPARATE RATE AFFECT THE COLLECTION OF STATE 
POLICY SURCHARGES? 
A. 
It would likely disrupt their collection.  Many state policy costs are collected through 
surcharges on delivery service.  For example, certain demand response costs, adjustments 
up or down associated with revenue decoupling mechanisms, recovery of certain deferrals, 
and NYSERDA Program costs, are examples of costs or adjustments passed through 
delivery surcharges.  Surcharges are not an insignificant portion of customers’ overall 
delivery charges and are necessary to achieve the overall retail cost allocation and rate 
design established in state regulatory proceedings.   
If a Large Load’s delivery service were replaced by an unbundled transmission rate, a 
surcharge on delivery might no longer be available as a collection mechanism, even though 
a retail sale would still be taking place and the State would retain jurisdiction over that 
retail sale.  The PSC might then have to change the collection mechanism, for example by 
reassigning those charges as commodity surcharges on the retail sale function.  Doing so 
would affect competitive ESCOs and LSEs and every customer class and would potentially 
require the PSC to reexamine cost recovery for dozens of programs.

Attachment I 
Page 25 of 29 
 
 
Q. 
WOULD AN UNBUNDLED TRANSMISSION RATE ELIMINATE THE NEED 
FOR STATE DELIVERY CHARGES? 
A. 
Whether an unbundled transmission rate would displace a PSC delivery rate is an open 
question.  If the Commission established a transmission rate but still permitted a 
distribution charge, the PSC would need to authorize utility re-designed delivery rates to 
remove transmission costs and to avoid double recovery.  If the Commission established a 
transmission rate and prohibited a delivery rate, Large Loads might no longer contribute to 
distribution, metering, surcharges, and overhead costs that the PSC has allocated to them, 
and those costs would shift to other customers.

THE INDICATED NYTOS’ REVISIONS TO ISO OATT SECTION 5 
Q. 
PLEASE SUMMARIZE THE INDICATED NYTOS’ PROPOSED REVISIONS TO 
SECTION 5. 
A. 
The revisions extend Section 5 to Eligible Customers serving Large Loads and reference 
the applicable PSC-approved, or LIPA Board of Trustees-approved, service classifications 
and delivery rates.7  The revised Section 5 details applicable delivery service classifications 
and rates for retail access service, including delivery service irrespective of whether a retail 
customer takes commodity supply from an ESCO or under a utility’s POLR obligation, and 
to Firm and Non-Firm Withdrawal Service for Eligible Customers on behalf of Large Loads 
under Attachment LL of the ISO OATT.  It also clarifies that Section 5 applies to Large 
Loads themselves to the extent they are Eligible Customers.   
 
7  
LIPA’s delivery service classifications and rates are subject to review and approval by the LIPA Board of 
Trustees.  Consistent with long-standing practice recognized by the Commission, LIPA rates are set forth in the ISO 
OATT section 5 are for informational purposes only.

Q. 
WHAT DO THE REVISIONS PROVIDE REGARDING THE CHARGES THAT 
APPLY TO LARGE LOADS? 
A. 
As reflected in the Revised Section 5.1.1, each retail access customer, including an Eligible 
Customer serving a Large Load, is responsible for paying the Retail Transmission Service 
Charge to the affected Transmission Owner consistent with the rates, terms and conditions 
of that Transmission Owner’s retail tariff, as approved under applicable State law and 
referenced in Sections 5.2 and 5.3.  An LSE serving the customer remains responsible for 
all applicable NYISO charges, including Transmission Usage Charges, billed under 
Section 2.7 and Attachment LL.  Revised Section 5.1.3 provides that each Transmission 
Owner may collect its Retail Transmission Service Charge directly from each customer 
that takes service under its retail tariffs, including Eligible Customers serving Large Loads, 
and that the rates, terms, and conditions are those of the applicable retail tariff approved by 
the PSC or the LIPA Board of Trustees. 
Q. 
WHAT OTHER CHANGES DO THE REVISIONS MAKE? 
A. 
The revisions update each company-specific description in Section 5.2 to cite the current 
PSC tariffs and to note the applicability to Eligible Customers serving Large Loads under 
Attachment LL.  New Section 5.2.8 sets out the rates, terms, and conditions of service for 
Eligible Customers taking service on behalf of Large Loads and lists the applicable service 
classifications for each Transmission Owner.  New Section 5.2.9 reserves each 
Transmission Owner’s right to modify its rates, terms, and conditions, subject to required 
approvals or filings under the New York Public Service Law, the New York Public 
Authorities Law, or the FPA as applicable.  The revisions also require Eligible Customers 
to satisfy applicable interconnection requirements, including under Attachments HH and

Attachment I 
Page 27 of 29 
 
 
LL, and require Eligible Customers serving Large Loads to execute the form of 
Transmission Service Agreement attached to the ISO OATT.  In addition, a new Section 
5.3 has been added to reference cost responsibility for Large Loads as further embodied by 
the Large Load Cost Recovery Agreement (“CRA”) included at Section 44.16.9 (Appendix 
9) in the NYISO OATT to be executed between a Connecting Transmission Owner or 
Affected Transmission Owner and the Large Load Project.  Newly created section 5.4.1 
requires Transmission Owners to apply revenue credits or adjustments to prevent double 
recovery of costs recovered under CRAs through FERC-jurisdictional wholesale 
transmission rates.  Finally, newly created section 5.4.2 requires Transmission Owners to 
file an annual informational report with FERC and the PSC to identify CRA revenues

credits have been or will be applied.  
VIII. THE NYISO’S COMPANION FILING 
Q. 
WHAT DOES THE NYISO’S COMPANION SECTION 205 FILING PROPOSE? 
A. 
The NYISO’s filing proposes new Attachment LL to the ISO OATT, including, inter alia, 
new Firm Withdrawal Service and Non-Firm Withdrawal Service for Eligible Customers 
serving Large Loads. 
Q. 
HOW DO THE INDICATED NYTOS’ SECTION 5 REVISIONS RELATE TO THE 
NYISO’S FILING? 
A. 
The two filings are complementary.  The NYISO’s charges do not address the embedded 
cost delivery charges that the utility holding the retail franchise applies under its PSC-
authorized service classifications.  Revised Section 5 fills that role by identifying the 
delivery rates that apply to Eligible Customers serving Large Loads, whether they take

Attachment I 
Page 28 of 29 
 
 
Firm or Non-Firm Withdrawal Service.  Together, the filings specify every charge a Large 
Load will pay:  NYISO market and ancillary charges under the NYISO’s tariffs, and 
embedded cost delivery charges under the referenced retail tariffs. 
Q. 
DOES CURTAILMENT OF A LARGE LOAD UNDER THE NYISO’S NON-FIRM 
SERVICE NECESSARILY REFLECT THE TRANSMISSION OWNER’S COST 
TO PROVIDE DELIVERY SERVICE? 
A. 
No.  A Large Load that is using Non-Firm Withdrawal Service may be curtailed by the 
NYISO because of conditions on the Bulk Power System that are unrelated to the 
Connecting Transmission Owner’s obligation to deliver energy.  The Connecting 
Transmission Owner may be planning and building its local system to serve that Large 
Load as a firm customer, consistent with the service the customer requested.  The pendency 
of firm service awaiting a non-local upgrade on an Affected Transmission Owner’s system 
may thus have nothing to do with how the Connecting Transmission Owner provides 
delivery service.  That is another reason why a discounted non-firm delivery rate, keyed to 
NYISO curtailments, would not necessarily reflect cost causation. 
Q. 
IS THERE TIME TO DEVELOP NEW RATES, IF ANY ARE NEEDED, BEFORE 
THE NYISO’S NEW SERVICES TAKE EFFECT? 
A. 
Yes.  The terms of the NYISO’s Non-Firm Withdrawal Service have been evolving until 
very recently.  Under the NYISO’s proposal, the earliest that new Non-Firm Withdrawal 
Services would be available is for projects in the transition Large Load Integration Process 
cluster.  As filed, the NYISO’s process would result in Facilities Study completion and 
security posting during or after the third quarter of 2028, which should precede service to

new rates that prove appropriate.

For each billing period, the customer’s total energy supply cost will be calculated as the sum of: (1) the hourly 
DAM multiplied by the customer’s hourly measured loads, as adjusted by the Factor of Adjustment set forth 
in General Information Section 29, and (2) the HPP UCAP Charge per kWh multiplied by the customer’s 
total measured load in kilowatthours. 
 
On and after May 1, 2011, capacity charges will be recovered through a separate charge, HPP UCAP.  Each 
customer’s capacity charge will be calculated as the product of the customer’s demand during the previous 
summer’s ICAP market peak hour, as adjusted pursuant to the ICAP market peak load forecast for the 
corresponding capability period and NYISO UCAP requirements, and the monthly NYISO Spot Auction 
price for the capacity zone(s) from which the capacity is acquired pursuant to the requirements of the NYISO 
for the prior calendar month.  The HPP UCAP will be stated in whole $0.01 amounts per kilowatt and will 
be filed with the Public Service Commission on the Statement of Market Price Charge and Market Price 
Adjustment.    
 
The HPP UCAP Charge will be renamed the HPP Charge and will continue to recover charges for energy 
balancing, ancillary services, allowances for working capital and bad debts according to the provisions 
provided above. 
 
Effective April 1, 2017, the HPP Charge will be increased by a component designed to recover or refund the 
costs or benefits of Renewable Energy Credits (REC’s), Zero Emissions Credits (ZEC’s) and Alternative 
Compliance Payments (ACP’s) for obligation years 2024 and prior, and the sale and transfer of Tier 1 VDER 
RECs  pursuant to Case 15-E-0302. Pursuant to Case 18-E-0071, the HPP Charge shall also be increased to 
reflect the costs of Offshore Wind Renewable Energy Credits (OREC’s). In addition, pursuant to Case 15-E-
0751, the CDG H-Value compliance obligation including associated carrying charges calculated at the other 
customer capital rate will be recovered through this component. The REC/ZEC/ACP component, including 
an allowance for bad debts will be determined on an annual basis. A reconciliation of recoveries (eleven 
months actual, one month forecast) will also be performed annually, with any over or under recoveries 
included in the development of succeeding rates. Total costs will be divided by an estimate of billed sales for 
the collection period. The factor so determined will be stated in whole $0.00001 amounts per kilowatt-hour 
and will be filed on the Statement of Market Price Charges. The REC/ZEC/OREC/ACP component shall be 
filed to become effective with the eighth billing batch of April. 
 
For billing purposes, REC/ZEC/OREC/ACP cost recovery will be included in the HPP Charge, with the 
combined amount shown as one line item on customer bills until December 31, 2024, after which the ACP 
cost recovery will no longer be included in the HPP charge. 
 
Effective November 1, 2017, the HPP Charge will be increased by a component designed to recover the 
market value of the compensation paid to customers under General Information Section 48.B for the 
Environmental Component related to the purchase of generation.  This component will be determined by 
taking the market value of the compensation paid and dividing by the estimate of full service sales, including 
HPP sales, as described in General Information Section 29 until December 31, 2024, after which the 
Environmental Component will be removed from the HPP charge and recovered through the REC charge. 
 
For each billing period, the customer’s total energy supply cost will be calculated as the sum of: (1) the hourly 
DAM multiplied by the customer’s hourly measured loads, as adjusted by the Factor of Adjustment set forth 
in General Information Section 29, (2) the customer’s HPP UCAP, and (3) the HPP Charge per kWh 
multiplied by the customer’s total measured load in kilowatthours.

application subject to any additional processing time required by the NYISO.  Customers may terminate 
service under this Special Provision upon written notice to the Company. 
 
 
Definitions 
 
The following definitions are applicable under this Special Provision: 
 
 
Bid: The customer’s load reduction nomination in kW for the Dispatch Day. 
 
Bidding Day: The day on which the customer submits its Bid to the Company, two days prior to the 
Dispatch Day. 
 
Calculated Load Reduction: The difference between the Customer Baseline Load and the customer’s actual 
metered load on an hourly basis.  The Calculated Load Reduction shall not be less than zero. 
 
Customer Baseline Load (CBL): Average hourly energy consumption, rounded to the nearest kWh, for 
each of the 24 hours in a day calculated in accordance with the NYISO methodology. 
 
Demand Reduction Bus: The electrical location where the load reduction will take place and where 
Locational Based Marginal Price (LBMP) is measured.  Each customer will be assigned to a specific 
Demand Reduction Bus for the entire term of service.

Criteria for Bids

level specified by the Company, subject to the zonal floor bid price

in 100 KW increments per account.  The Company will aggregate bids and submit

The aggregation of Bids into 1 MW increments may require adjustments to the
bid price level, which may reduce the competitiveness of the Company's bid to
the NYISO.  If aggregated Bids on any Demand Reduction Bus are less than 1 MW,
the Company will reject all Bids at that Demand Reduction Bus.  Prior to 5
A.M. on the Notification Day, the Company will submit its bids to the NYISO. 
Between 11 A.M. and 3 P.M., on the Notification Day, the Company will notify
the customer which Bids are accepted.  Any Bid not accepted is deemed
rejected.
Rates and Charges
The customer will be subject to all other rates and charges in this Service
Classification.

SERVICE CLASSIFICATION NO. 14  
 
 
STANDBY SERVICE  
 
 
APPLICABLE TO USE OF SERVICE FOR: 
 
All purposes, where a customer operates on-site generation (OSG) with a total nameplate rating greater than, or expected 
to be greater than, fifteen percent (15%) of its maximum potential demand served by all sources, and determined in the 
same manner as the Contract Demand set forth below, and where the customer elects to have the Company supply and/or 
deliver energy to the customer by means of the Company's delivery facilities.  For purposes of this Service 
Classification, OSG shall be defined as a generation facility which does not supply energy to the customer by means of 
the Company’s delivery facilities and “delivery facilities” shall mean any facilities or equipment that are part of the 
Company’s electrical system regardless of the voltage level or functional classification. 
 
Customers taking service under a metered service classification and not otherwise required to take Standby Service may 
“opt-in” to the rates offered under this Service Classification, as described in Special Provision 14.12. 
 
With the exceptions listed below, OSG customers who decline service under this tariff are required to electrically isolate 
themselves from the Company’s electric system and the Company will not be required to maintain or supply service to 
such customers.  A customer shall be considered electrically isolated if (a) the electrical points of contact where 
interconnection may occur are separated and at least one-hundred (100) feet from any other interconnected electrical 
service of such customer, or (b) the disconnected isolated service is not within the same building or structure as any other 
interconnected electrical services of the customer and not housed within a common enclosure with other interconnected 
breakers and/or fuses of the customer. 
 
STANDBY SERVICE IS NOT APPLICABLE TO: 
 
Standby service shall not be applicable in the following instances, and shall be so designated in the customer’s 
Application for Electric Standby Service, as applicable: 
 
Non-Material Operation of On-Site Generation 
 
Central Hudson shall have the right to exclude a customer from this Service Classification upon any appropriate grounds, 
including, without limitation, a demonstration that the customer (a) has installed OSG with a total nameplate rating 
greater than fifteen percent (15%) of its load, but (b) has not operated or is not operating that OSG in a material manner 
in order to serve the customer's load.

CONTRACT DEMAND 
 
A customer opting into these rates  under Special Provision 14.12 shall have their contract demand initially set at the 
maximum metered demand over the previous twelve (12) months measured based on the highest rolling 60 minute 
integrated demand established during the monthly period for Service Classification No 1, 2 non-demand, and 6 and 
measured based on the highest 15 minute integrated demand for all other customers. For customers without twelve 
months of metered demand history, the contract demand shall be initially set at the maximum metered demand over 
the entire billing history, measured based on the highest 60-minute or 15-minute integrated demand, as applicable, 
and may be adjusted upward each month until a maximum over the previous twelve months is established. 
 
Non-mass market customers that operate on-site generation will have the option of: 
 
1) 
establishing their own Contract Demand, and providing this nomination in writing to the Company 
at least ten (10) days prior to the first day of the customer's next billing cycle, for existing 
customers, or at least ten (10) days prior to commencing service, for new customers; or 
 
2) 
accepting a Contract Demand established by Central Hudson in accordance with the following: 
 
(a) 
In the case of an existing customer, the Contract Demand shall initially be set at the 
maximum metered demand over the previous twelve (12) months; 
 
(b) 
In the case of a new customer, the Contract Demand shall be determined by assessing the 
nameplate rating of the equipment to be served, and projecting the coincidence and 
diversity of the new customer's load.  The Contract Demand so determined shall be 
provided to the customer, in writing, at least ten (10) days prior to the customer 
commencing service. 
 
 
The Contract Demand may be increased by the customer at any time with written notice to the Company.  Such 
notice must be provided at least ten (10) days prior to the first day of the customer's next billing cycle. 
 
For customers whose parent service classification is Service Classification No. 1, 2 non-demand or 6, the monthly 
demand will be the highest rolling 60-minute integrated kilowatt demand established during the monthly period for 
which a bill is rendered. For all other customers, the monthly demand will be the highest 15-minute integrated 
kilowatt demand established during the monthly period for which a bill is rendered.  For all instances where the 
customer's actual metered monthly demand exceeds the customer's Contract Demand, the customer's Contract 
Demand will be increased to the new peak.  If, in any given billing month, there is a failure in meter data acquisition 
that results in the failure to measure the actual monthly peak demand, the Contract Demand shall be used for billing 
and recording purposes.  
 
If the customer demonstrates that electricity-producing equipment has been removed or disabled in place or 
appropriate load limiting devices are installed and operated, the Contract Demand may be reduced upon written 
request from the customer and written acknowledgment of the request from the Company, except that if the 
Company does not accept or reject the request within ten (10) days of its receipt, the request shall be deemed 
granted.  Such notice must be provided at least ten (10) days prior to the first day of the customer's next billing 
cycle.

HOURLY PRICING PROVISION 
 
All customers electing to purchase their energy requirements from the Company will be billed for these 
requirements based on the charges set on an hourly basis according to the market price of electricity described 
below.  
 
The market price of electricity will be the hourly Day-Ahead Locational Based Market Price (DAM) as set forth by 
the New York State Independent System Operator (NYISO) for Central Hudson, Hudson Valley, Zone G (Zone G). 
The source of the hourly prices will be the NYISO website for the DAM. 
 
OTHER CHARGES 
 
Customers taking service under this Service Classification will also be subject to charges for energy balancing as 
well as non-energy components of electric power supply, such as capacity, ancillary services and allowances for 
working capital costs and bad debts. 
 
Capacity charges will be recovered through a separate charge, HPP UCAP. Each customer’s capacity charge will be 
calculated as the product of the customer’s demand during the previous summer’s ICAP market peak hour, as 
adjusted pursuant to the ICAP market peak load forecast for the corresponding capability period and NYISO UCAP 
requirements, and the monthly NYISO Spot Auction price for the capacity zone(s) from which the capacity is 
acquired pursuant to the requirements of the NYISO for the prior calendar month. The HPP UCAP will be stated in 
whole $0.01 amounts per kilowatt and will be filed with the Public Service Commission on the Statement of Market 
Price Charge and Market Price Adjustment. 
 
For customers without metered demand during the previous summer’s ICAP market peak hour, such demand shall 
be determined as follows: 
1) 
Customers whose parent service classification is SC No. 1, 2 or 6 will utilize the demand of the 
customer’s respective load profile, adjusted for the customer’s specific usage factor; or 
(2) 
Customers whose parent service classification is SC No. 3 or 13, the demand will be estimated by 
the Company on the basis of available data; and 
(3) 
For customers in (1) or (2) above with OSG, the estimated demand will be reduced by an estimate 
of the output of the generator based on: 
(a)  the National Renewable Laboratory Photovoltaic Profiles (“NREL Profiles”) included in       
Appendix H of the Commission’s September 14, 2017 Order in Case 15-E-0751for solar; or  
(b) rated capacity and anticipated usage of equipment for other technologies; and 
(4) 
For customers with estimated demand during the previous summer’s ICAP market peak hour, 
actual metered demand during the previous summer’s ICAP market peak hour will be utilized 
beginning May 1 of the year following the ICAP market peak hour for which the customer had 
metered demand. 
 
The HPP Charge will recover charges for energy balancing, ancillary services, allowances for working capital and 
bad debts. 
 
INCREASE IN RATES AND CHARGES 
 
All rates and charges billed under this Service Classification, including the Minimum Charge, and other charges 
pursuant to the General Information Section (as applicable), shall be increased pursuant to General Information 
Section 30 to reflect the tax rates applicable within the municipality where the customer takes service.

Customers with OSG that enters service after July 29, 2003, and uses any of the designated technologies 
listed below shall have the option of: (a) an exemption from the standby rates of this Service Classification

fuels does not include the combustion or electrolysis of fossil fuels, or the use of fossil fuel or

photovoltaics; 5) hydroelectric; 6) tidal; 7) geothermal electric; 8) geothermal ground source heat; 9) wave 
energy; and 10) ocean thermal. Customers with sustainably managed biomass, biogas, and fuel cell units 
which utilize fossil fuel resources that enters service between July 29, 2003 and May 31, 2023, inclusive, 
are included as a designated technology.

A customer who installs a new combined heat and power (CHP) system 
(1) on or after June 1, 2015 and before May 31, 2021; 
(2) with a capacity greater than 1 MW and less than 15 MW; and, 
(3) that would otherwise be subject to the standby rates of this Service Classification 
 
shall have the option of (a) a one-time exemption from the standby rates of this Service 
 
Classification by taking service at the standard rates of the applicable Parent Service 
 
Classification; or (b) service at the standby rates of this Service Classification. 
 
A customer meeting the aforementioned requirements is required to install, at the customer’s expense, a 
revenue grade, interval meter to measure generation output with telecommunications capability at their on-
site facility.  The interval meter must be compatible with the Company’s metering infrastructure, and the 
customer must provide and maintain all meter communications services.  In cases where the Company is 
unable to read the meter through the customer provided telecommunications equipment, and the Company 
has determined that the problem is not caused by the Company’s equipment, the customer will be assessed 
an $80.00 on-site meter reading charge each meter reading cycle until the condition is corrected. 
 
A customer meeting the aforementioned requirements will have the opportunity to exercise between June 1, 
2015 and May 31, 2021, inclusive, a one-time election to be exempt from the standby rates of this Service 
Classification.  Once elected (a) such exemption will be effective for four years running from the in-service 
date of the system, or (b) the customer may exercise the option to exit the exemption one time prior to the 
end of its four-year exemption period. 
 
Upon expiration of the exemption or exercise of the option to exit the exemption, the customer will be 
subject to the standby rates of this Service Classification as they may be modified or superseded as 
approved by the Public Service Commission.

14.11 
Standby Reliability Credit  
 
The Standby Reliability Credit shall not apply to customers billed under the revised Standby Service rates 
pursuant to case 15-E-0751 except for customers initiating service under this Service Classification prior to 
March 16, 2022. A Standby Reliability Credit (“Credit”) is available to Customers taking service under this 
service classification, excluding customers with stand-alone storage as referenced in General Information 
Section 48.B. Such credit will be available for service taken under this service classification during a 
previous Measurement Period for which interval metered data was available. The Credit will be earned 
when a Standby Customer reduces their load below their Contract Demand, over two consecutive Summer 
Periods in which interval metered data is available during defined Measurement Periods. In the event that a 
Customer does not yet have interval metered data available, they may determine their own maximum 
anticipated demand (net of load reduction or generation assets) pursuant to the Contract Demand provisions 
of this service classification for use in the calculation. The Credit will be equal to the difference between 
the Standby Customer’s Contract Demand in kW, and their highest kW demand recorded on the 
Customer’s interval meter (net of generation) during the previous Measurement Period, multiplied by the 
Contract Demand Delivery Charge per kW that is in effect on October 1 of the year in which the credit is 
determined. The Credit will be applied to the Customer’s successive 12 monthly bills commencing in 
November until the following October.  
 
A Customer seeking a Credit must request such Credit by October 14 of each year for which the Credit is 
sought and, at the same time, specify the Outage Events that the Customer requests to be excluded from the 
Measurement Period. If October 14 falls on a weekend or holiday, the Company will accept requests until 
the next business day. If service is taken under the Multi-Party Offset of Special Provision 14.10, the Credit 
will be applied to the Recipient Account in the Sponsor’s name; provided, however, that if the Sponsor has 
more than one Recipient Account in its name, the Credit will be applied to the Sponsor’s account which has 
the highest Contract Demand. 
 
If the Customer is billed under Special Provision 14.10, the kW to be credited on each Standby Service 
account supplied by the generating facility’s output will be based on the total kW to be credited multiplied 
by the ratio of the Contract Demand on the Standby Service account to the aggregated Contract Demands 
on all the Standby Service accounts supplied by the generating facility’s output. 
 
If service is taken under the Multi-Party Offset of Special Provision 14.10, the Credit for any Measurement 
Period will be equal to the product of: (a) and the difference between the customer’s contract demand and 
customer’s highest recorded demand during the Measurement Period, excluding Outage Events, and (b) the 
Contract Demand Delivery Charge per kW that is in effect on October 14 of the year in which the Credit is 
determined.

comprised of no more than five 24-hour time periods, excluding weekends and holidays. If a time 
block contains a time period of less than 24 hours, the time period will be rounded up to the next 
24 hours. 24-hour periods cannot be applied on a partial basis. If a time block encompasses a 
holiday or weekend, the start of the 24-hour period on the day prior to the holiday weekend until 
the same hour the next business day will be considered to be a single 24-hour period.

required to remain on Standby Service rates for a minimum of twelve months.

Service Classification. and be subject to incremental metering charge applicable under the Hourly Pricing 
Provision of the tariff if the customer is required under their parent service classification. 
 
Term 
A customer taking service under this Special Provision may discontinue service under this Service 
Classification at any time, but will not be able to opt back into Standby Service for a minimum of one year.

4. Reactive Demand Charges - Rate Codes 284, 285, M284, and M285 
 
a) Transmission and primary service Customers who use electricity at a Power Factor of 
less than 90% and choose to pay a monthly Reactive Demand Charge of $0.27 per 
KVAR, shall pay for the additional metering equipment either when it is installed or 
through a monthly charge.  
 
b) For the first twelve (12) months of billing for Reactive Demand Charges, the KVAR 
charges will not exceed 1% of the Customer's total bill. 
 
5. How Demand is Determined 
 
The Authority will furnish and maintain a demand meter of standard type to determine the 
demand. The demand is the maximum 15-minute demand during the month in each Rate 
Period, taken to the nearest one-tenth (1/10) kilowatt. 
 
6. How the Minimum Demand Charges are Determined - All Rate Codes 
 
a) The Authority will charge an annual Minimum Demand Charge to those Customers 
whose actual billed demand revenues in Periods 1, 2, and 3 are less than the Minimum 
Demand Charges given below. The Authority will not apply this charge to new Customers 
taking service for part of a calendar year or Customer-generators eligible for net billing. 
 
b) The Authority will use the highest recorded demands for Periods 1, 2, and 3 and multiply 
those demands by the Minimum Demand Charges to determine the minimum amount the 
Customer is responsible for.   
 
c) If the sum of the Minimum Demand Charges in the three (3) Periods is greater than the 
sum of the actual billed demand revenues for the year under review, the difference will be 
charged to the Customer's account, and 
 
d) When this difference is more than ten percent (10%) of the total annual demand 
revenues, the Customer may choose to pay it in no more than twelve (12) equal monthly 
installments.

7. How the Net Reactive Demand is Determined 
 
a) The Net Reactive Demand is the 15-minute integrated kilovolt-amperes of lagging 
reactive demand minus 48% of the 15-minute integrated kilowatt demand recorded 
during the same 15-minute period. 
 
b) The Customer will be billed monthly for the maximum Net Reactive Demand recorded 
between 7:00 a.m. through 11:00 p.m. 
 
c) For billing purposes, the maximum Net Reactive Demand will be the greater of:  
 
(1) The maximum Net Reactive Demand recorded for the month from 7:00 a.m. through 
11:00 p.m., or   
 
(2) 100% of the maximum Net Reactive Demand recorded from June through 
September, from 7:00 a.m. through 11:00 p.m., during the last eleven (11) months. 
 
8. Terms of Payment 
 
The Customer shall pay the balance due in cash, including checks and money orders, on 
receiving the bill. Late payments shall be subject to Late Payment Charges.  
 
9. Term of Service 
 
a) The Authority will provide service to the Customer for at least one (1) year and until 
service is terminated either by the Customer or the Authority.  
 
b) The Customer shall give the Authority thirty (30) days written notice when requesting 
termination of service. 
 
c) The Authority may terminate service to the Customer in accordance with the provisions of 
the Tariff, after giving the Customer thirty (30) days written notice. 
 
d) The Authority may require the Customer to take service at rates effective for a longer 
term because of the investment required or other unusual conditions related to the 
service.

1. Who Is Eligible  
 
This Service Classification (SC-12) is applicable to Customers meeting the requirements of 
(a) through (d) below (Standby Service Customers) and Customers meeting the requirements 
of (e) through (f) below (Optional Rate Customers): 
 
Standby Service 
 
a)  Customers who have generation installed on their site, whether the generation equipment 
is owned by the customer or a third party; or 
 
b)  Customers who are directly interconnected with a Generator, as defined as a company 
whose primary business is the production of electricity; 
 
c)  Generators who require service from the Authority when their own electric generating 
equipment is not sufficient to meet their own load; or 
 
d)  Customers with on-site generation compensated under Value Stack, that meet the 
requirements for compensation, and that are not otherwise exempt in accordance with 
Section P.4 of this SC-12. 
 
Optional Rate Service 
 
e) Customers that opt into SC-12, who do not otherwise meet the requirements of Standby 
Service (Optional Rate Customers).  Any customer may opt into SC-12 with the exception 
of SC-5, SC-7, SC-10, SC-13 customers, unmetered customers and non-AMI metered 
customers. Optional Rate Customers can switch back to applicable non-Standby rates 
available to them at any time, however, to avoid customers switching to take advantage 
of seasonal fluctuations in rate design, Optional Rate Customers that switch back to a 
non-time-varying flat rate will not be allowed on Standby rates or other time-varying rate 
code for a period of not less than one year. 
 
f) 
Customers on ReCharge NY service will be assigned to Rate 680 and cannot opt-in to 
Standby Rates. 
 
g) More specifically, Standby Service shall apply to: 
 
 
(1)  Customers with on-site generation serving load that is not isolated from the grid;  
 
 
(2)  Generators that rely on the Authority to serve electric loads that would otherwise be 
served by the generator such as station power used for the heating, lighting, air-
conditioning, and office equipment needs of the buildings housing the generator and 
associated support facilities located on a generating facility’s site, and/or to facilitate the 
re-starting of the generator following an outage. Standby rates will also apply to 
Generators that take station power through the same bus bar as they supply the grid.   
  
h) For Standby Service Customers, the Parent Service Classification shall be defined based 
upon the applicable Contract Demand at the delivery point (as initially calculated by the 
Authority).

i) 
Same Bus Bar 
 
Same Bus Bar is defined as a common electrical point of interconnection on the same 
physical bus bar structure located at one substation of the utility and an individual 
customer’s system at the single voltage level at which the customer takes service. This 
common point of interconnection may include up to one load serving connection, or tap, 
(such tap is in addition to the single point of delivery service from the generating 
customer to the Authority’s delivery system being metered), from a single physical bus 
bar (one tap must be connecting the customer's generation output to the bus and a 
second tap must be connecting the customer's electric service to the bus) located at an 
Authority substation. The customer’s generation must be on a single unitary tract of land; 
adjoining and abutting the land upon which the Authority substation is located and the 
points of delivery and receipt must not be more than 500 feet apart. The presence of 
Authority equipment, including but not limited to switches, fuses, transformers, and circuit 
breakers, between the point(s) of delivery is not considered Same Bus Bar.

4. Exemptions From SC-12 
 
The following customers shall not be subject to SC-12, but shall be served under the 
customer's otherwise applicable service classification unless Customers make a one-time 
irrevocable election to forfeit or refuse the exemption and join the Standby Rate or the in 
progress Phase-In period of Standby Rates, identified in SC-12.14.g if still applicable.  
Customers that qualify for the Environmentally Advantageous Technologies (EAT) Exemption 
and that request a one-time irrevocable election to join Standby Rates or the in progress 
Phase-In period for Standby Rates if still applicable, will make the request by providing thirty 
(30) days written notice to the Authority before commencing operation of the OSG. 
 
a) Small Generators 
 
Customers with a nameplate aggregate generator(s) 5 kVA or smaller that may run in 
parallel with the LIPA system. 
 
b) Customers with On-Site Generators (OSG) Less than or Equal to 15% of Maximum 
Potential Demand as identified in SC-12.14.e. 
 
c) Environmentally Advantageous Technologies (EAT) Exemptions 
Customers who install OSG that are: 
 
(1) Solar thermal;  
(2) Solar photovoltaic;  
(3) Onshore and offshore wind; 
(4) Hydroelectric; 
(5) Geothermal electric; 
(6) Geothermal ground source heat; 
(7) Tidal energy; 
(8) Wave energy; 
(9) Ocean thermal;

11 Determination of Contract Demand  
 
a) Contract Demand for Standby Service Customers  
 
Contract Demand shall initially be set at the maximum anticipated demand of the 
customer including any load that is not isolated referenced in the Standby Service 
Application and determined as the greater of the following and the Authority shall inform 
the customer of the resultant contract demand ten (10) days prior to the next billing cycle: 
 
(1) the maximum demand from the Authority's system over the previous 12-months, or 
(2) the customer's maximum load supplied by all sources including the OSG and 
Authority's supply system over the previous 12-months. 
 
In the case of a new customer (i.e., a customer for whom historical consumption data 
does not exist), the Contract Demand shall be the maximum anticipated demand of load 
consumed as prescribed in the customer’s load letter.   
 
The Contract Demand shall automatically be increased to the highest measured demand 
in any billing period during the term hereunder.    
 
The Contract Demand of a Generator who is connected to a customer which would 
otherwise be served directly by the Authority shall be set at the maximum potential 
demand of the station power of the Generator when the generator is out of service plus 
the maximum potential demand of the customer. 
 
The Contract Demand may be increased based upon a written notice by the customer to 
the Authority at any time. 
 
The Contract Demand as determined above may be reduced based upon a written 
request by the customer to the Authority. Contract Demand requests may be made no 
more than one time in a 365-day period and/or 365 days from any increase or ratchet in 
Contract Demand. In the event the customer’s Contract Demand request is accepted by 
the Authority and the Contract Demand is reduced; if thereafter the recorded maximum 
demand at any time exceeds the customer's requested Contract Demand: (i) by 20% or 
greater than a penalty equal to the product of 24 times the Contract Demand rate times 
the demand in excess of the Contract Demand shall apply, (ii) by 10% or greater, but less 
than 20%, then a penalty equal to the product of 18 times the Contract Demand rate 
times the demand in excess of the Contract Demand shall apply, (iii) by less than 10% 
then a penalty equal to the product of 12 times the Contract Demand rate times the 
demand in excess of the Contract Demand shall apply.  
 
Seasonal or other temporary fluctuations in load of the customer's existing facilities such 
as heating and air conditioning, and temporary reductions in manufacturing shall not 
qualify for reductions in the Contract Demand. 
 
The effective date of the revised Contract Demand shall be the next billing cycle following 
the Authority's receipt of the customer's written notice provided such notice is received 10 
business days prior to the first day of the next billing cycle.

b) Contract Demand for Optional Rate Customers  
 
Contract Demand will be established initially as the customer’s maximum measured

automatically be increased to the highest measured demand in any billing period during 
the term hereunder. In the event the customer has installed energy efficient equipment or

of the Contract Demand by the Authority. Any reduction of the Contract Demand will be at 
the Authority’s discretion.  
 
c) As Used Off-Peak Daily Demand  
 
The As-Used Off-peak Daily Demand shall be the aggregate of the highest daily 15-
minute integrated demand (measured in kW) occurring during the off-peak hours of each 
day during the billing period, except for customers of parent service classification is SC-1 
or SC-2 Small non-demand it shall be the aggregate of the highest 60-minute integrated 
demand (measured in kW) during the off-peak hours of each day during the billing period. 
 
Off-Peak hours are defined as follows: During the months of October through May, for the 
hours between 8:00 am and 10:00 pm, daily. During the months of June through 
September, for the hours between 8:00 am and 3:00 pm and 7:00 pm through 10:00 pm, 
Mondays through Fridays, and 8:00 am through 10:00 pm, Saturdays, Sundays and 
Federal Holidays.  
 
d) As Used Peak Daily Demand  
 
The As-Used Peak Daily Demand shall be the aggregate of the highest daily 15-minute 
integrated demand (measured in kW) occurring during the peak hours of each day during 
the billing period, except for customers of parent service classification is SC-1 or SC-2 
Small non-demand it shall be the aggregate of the highest 60-minute integrated demand 
(measured in kW) during the peak hours of each day during the billing period.  
 
Peak hours are defined as follows: During the months of June through September, for the 
hours between 3:00 pm and 7:00 pm, Mondays through Fridays, excluding Federal 
Holidays.

12. Interconnection Requirements 
 
a) The Authority may disconnect a Customer from the system if the Customer operates a 
generator in parallel with the Authority’s system without an Interconnection Agreement 
(IA) with the Authority. 
  
b) The Customer must sign an IA within ninety (90) days of written notice, including a draft 
IA, from the Authority, unless 
 
c) The Customer has filed a complaint following the Consumer Complaint Procedures in 
Section VI of the Tariff. In this case, the Customer will not be disconnected until the 
complaint is resolved, unless the parallel generation creates a hazardous condition or 
threatens the integrity of the system.  
 
d) The facility may be connected for parallel operation with the service of the Authority, or 
isolated for operation with Standby Service provided by a Wholesale Generator by means 
of a double throw transfer switch or transfer switching scheme acceptable to the 
Authority. 
 
e) Customers with an OSG and connected for parallel operation with the service of the 
Authority are required to execute an IA with the Authority.  Customers having an OSG in 
aggregate with other OSGs of less than 10 MW are eligible to apply the service using the 
SGIP. Customers without an OSG are not required to execute an IA with the Authority. 
All other customers must execute an Interconnection Agreement, available from Authority 
representatives.
